analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give full cash refunds for canceled or significantly delayed flights and for passenger cancellations made 48 hours ahead.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large airlines and ticket sellers to offer passengers a full cash refund — including any fees — when the airline cancels or significantly delays a flight, or when the passenger cancels at least 48 hours before departure. Airlines could still offer vouchers instead, but only if they clearly told passengers they had a right to cash and the voucher never expired. It would also have let passengers retroactively swap unused pandemic-era vouchers for cash, and required disclosure before purchase that tickets are refundable.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers who get stranded by cancellations and delays, and passengers holding unused vouchers from flights canceled during the COVID-19 pandemic, which could be converted to cash.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a full cash refund, including ancillary fees, within 30 days of a request when a covered carrier cancels or significantly delays a flight, or when the passenger cancels at least 48 hours before departure [S2, S3].

If an airline offers a voucher or credit instead of cash, the bill requires a clear and conspicuous notice of the passenger's right to cash, and the voucher must remain valid indefinitely — addressing complaints that airline vouchers expire quickly [S2, S3].
Passengers who received vouchers for flights canceled between March 2020 and enactment could request a cash refund for any portion not yet used [S3].
Before selling a ticket, carriers and ticket agents must disclose in writing that the passenger can cancel at any time for any reason and get a full cash refund [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large passenger airlines (those with over $1.5 billion in 2018 revenue) and foreign carriers flying to or from the U.S., which would owe refunds and face $1,000 civil penalties per violation. Ticket agents must pass refunds through but get reimbursement from the carrier.

drawbacks.text: The refund obligation is limited to one flight per passenger per city-pair itinerary per day, so passengers with multi-flight trips would not get cash for every leg [S3].
The bill allows airlines to keep offering vouchers as an alternative, so carriers could still push passengers toward credit rather than cash as long as notices and no-expiration terms are met [S2].

The bill would let airlines pay for the refunds using COVID-era industry relief funds appropriated after March 2020 (though not the CARES Act payroll-support money under section 4112), effectively directing federal pandemic aid toward refund obligations [S3].
The penalty is a $1,000 civil penalty per violation payable to the government, which is small relative to ticket volumes and may not deter widespread noncompliance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers, the benefits are concrete: cash instead of expiring vouchers when an airline strands you, and cash back on unused pandemic vouchers. The costs fall on airlines, which would face refund liabilities they largely avoid today, though the bill's own carve-outs — one refund per itinerary per day, vouchers still allowed, modest penalties — soften the burden. The measure is modest in scope and would mainly matter during waves of mass cancellations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Cash Refunds for Flight Cancellations Act of 2022 on July 28, 2022, joined by three Democratic cosponsors — Sens. Blumenthal, Warren, and Whitehouse [S3, S4].
The same day it was introduced, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action was ever taken [S5].
With no markup, hearing, or vote recorded in the action history, the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large airlines and ticket agents are better off because the bill never moved: they keep the existing system in which refunds for canceled flights often come as vouchers or credits, and passengers who accepted pandemic-era vouchers cannot convert unused balances to cash. In fairness, Congress did later address airline refunds through other legislation, but this bill itself died without a vote.

for.name: Sen. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cash Refunds for Flight Cancellations Act of 2022 and shepherded it to committee referral.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, and Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action — no markup, hearing, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four senators attached to the bill were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one had to go on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would have required cash refunds for canceled and significantly delayed flights — an obligation airlines largely avoid today, since they can typically steer stranded passengers into vouchers or rebooking. It would also have forced retroactive cash conversion of unused pandemic-era vouchers and allowed payment of refunds from COVID-era industry relief funds (excluding CARES Act payroll support).

industries.industry: Ticket agents and online travel sellers
industries.note: Ticket agents would face refund and disclosure duties but would be reimbursed by the airline for the carrier's share of the refunded fare, limiting their net cost to administrative burden.
